definition: Interactive activation and competition (IAC) networks are artificial neural networks used to model memory and intuitive generalizations.
details: They are made up of nodes or artificial neurons which are arrayed and activated in ways that emulate the behaviors of human memory. The IAC model is used by the parallel distributed processing (PDP) Group and is associated with James L. McClelland and David E. Rumelhart; it is described in detail in their book Explorations in Parallel Distributed Processing: A Handbook of Models, Programs, and Exercises. This model does not contradict any currently known biological data or theories, and its performance is close enough to human performance as to warrant further investigation.

explainer.lead: Interactive activation and competition networks are artificial neural networks built to model human memory and intuitive generalisation. They matter as a classic connectionist account of how memory behaviour can emerge from neuron-like nodes.

tiers.eli5: Think of a network of nodes that excite their friends and quiet their rivals, so the strongest pattern wins, much like how recalling one thing brings related things to mind.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers use IAC models to simulate memory phenomena with nodes arrayed and activated in neuron-like ways. A pitfall is treating such simulations as direct evidence of the brain's mechanisms rather than as models that merely avoid contradicting known biological data.
tiers.paperLevel: An IAC network consists of nodes or artificial neurons arrayed and activated in ways that emulate human memory behaviour, as described by McClelland and Rumelhart's PDP Group; the model does not contradict currently known biological data or theories.

explainer.example: An IAC model can be set up with units for concepts that mutually activate related units and inhibit competing ones, reproducing patterns of memory retrieval seen in human experiments.
